 Finance Massive tech sell-off has Nasdaq 100 entering another correction
 What’s got investors running scared? 
 By Matty Merritt October 31, 2026 • less than 3 min read
 TOPICS: Finance / Markets, Stocks & Investing Strategy / Market Volatility The state of the Nasdaq yesterday was as scary as encountering a group of teens in matching clown masks stocking up on eggs for an “omelet party.” The tech-heavy index suffered a huge hit over the last few days as investors faced their fears about tech companies’ massive AI spending after several reported less-than-stellar earnings this week.
 Correction territory. With tech stocks selling off, the Nasdaq Composite finished the day down 2.86%, its worst single-day performance since June. The Nasdaq 100 shed as much as 4.5% yesterday, falling into its third correction this year.
 What’s got investors running scared?
 Several Big Tech earnings reports this week led investors and analysts to come to a similar conclusion: A lot of money is going into AI and not enough is coming out. Plus, more traditional moneymakers weren’t delivering as much as hoped amid the spending spree:
 Google parent Alphabet’s stock had its worst day ever on Thursday, with about $475 billion in market value vanishing after it reported on Wednesday that search revenue growth was slower than expected, and free cash flow (i.e., the money left after paying for AI infrastructure like data centers) had swung to a ~$9 billion loss.
 Amazon’s stock fell 1.41% yesterday, after reporting on Thursday that it spent even more money than it expected on AI last quarter, and growth from its online shopping sector slowed down.
 Neocloud companies and chipmakers all fell this week. But no one is having a worse time than Intel. Its stock cratered 28.58% yesterday—its worst day in 50 years—after its Thursday earnings report revealed weak PC demand amid high AI spending. The US government’s 10% stake in the company lost about $12 billion yesterday, according to CNBC.
 Big picture: AI spending is having a big impact on the economy, and tech companies see it as their way to dominate in the future, but investors are getting nervous about whether it’s going to pay off.— MM
